findings.claim: All 48 practice questions, across all eight lessons, are typed “40 marks — Shakespeare Essay”.
findings.truth: Jane Eyre is the 19th-century prose set text on the modern and literary heritage paper. Shakespeare sits in the other component. Relabelled “40 marks — 19th-century prose essay”.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/english-literature-J352.md section 3a: Section B of the modern and literary heritage component is 19th century prose, 40 marks; Shakespeare is in the poetry and Shakespeare component.

findings.claim: All 48 mark ladders are malformed. Lesson 1 uses “Band 6: … / Lower bands: less detailed.”; lessons 2-8 use “Mastering / Secure / Developing / Emerging”.
findings.truth: Neither ladder uses house band names and neither scales to the real 40-mark total. Rescaled to five equal house bands: Top (33-40), Upper-mid (25-32), Mid (17-24), Lower-mid (9-16), Low (1-8), keeping each question's own top-band content.
findings.evidence: House ladder rule in CHECK_PROMPT.md; same rescale applied in the sibling unit english-literature-ocr__great-expectations.

findings.claim: The author's surname is spelt “Brönte” 211 times across lessons 2-8 (content 84, practice questions 104, exam tips 11, conclusions 9, knowledge checks 3). Lesson 1 spells it correctly.
findings.truth: Charlotte Brontë. Corrected everywhere with 104 unique-context text replacements plus whole-value replacements in the JSON fields.
findings.evidence: Author's name; lesson 1 of this same unit already spells it Brontë 25 times.

findings.claim: “Jane’s inheritance of £20,000 — which she divides among her cousins — gives her the financial independence to choose freely.”
findings.truth: She divides it four ways and keeps a quarter. Giving it all away would leave her with nothing, which contradicts the point the sentence makes.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 33: “Were we not four? Twenty thousand pounds shared equally would be five thousand each.” Ch. 37: “My uncle in Madeira is dead, and he left me five thousand pounds.”

findings.claim: “Jane fights back — ‘my habitual mood of humiliation… was gone’ — and is punished by being locked in the red room.”
findings.truth: Fabricated quotation that also reverses the sense. The mood returns and damps her anger, and it happens inside the red room, not while she fights.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 2: “My habitual mood of humiliation, self-doubt, forlorn depression, fell damp on the embers of my decaying ire.” The real resistance line is “I resisted all the way: a new thing for me”.

findings.claim: “He tells Miss Temple that the girls should not be fed ‘the fragile body’ and that privation will save their souls.”
findings.truth: Fabricated quotation. Brocklehurst's phrase is “vile bodies”, and the point is that feeding them well starves their souls.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 7: “you may indeed feed their vile bodies, but you little think how you starve their immortal souls!”

findings.claim: “his own family wear ‘false French curls’” (also in flashcard 9).
findings.truth: The phrase is “a false front of French curls” and it is worn by Mrs Brocklehurst.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 7: “the elder lady … wore a false front of French curls.”

findings.claim: “The girls walk two miles through ‘benumbing’ cold to church … punished for small ‘infractions of the rules.’”
findings.truth: Neither quoted word is in the novel. The two-mile walk to Brocklebridge Church is real; the wind “almost flayed the skin from our faces”.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 7; “benumb” and “infraction” return no matches in the whole text.

findings.claim: Helen Burns: “It is not violence that best overcomes hate… but reading the New Testament.” (content and flashcard 11).
findings.truth: Fabricated ending. Helen's line stops at “injury”; “Read the New Testament” is a separate answer two speeches later.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 6: “It is not violence that best overcomes hate—nor vengeance that most certainly heals injury.”

findings.claim: “Helen’s last words — ‘I am going to God’”, repeated in knowledge check 4 (“Helen Burns’s last words are…”) and flashcard 13 (“What are Helen’s final words to Jane?”).
findings.truth: “I am going to God” comes early in the night's conversation. Her last words are “Good-night, Jane.” The knowledge check and flashcard both taught the wrong fact.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 9: “‘I believe; I have faith: I am going to God’ … ‘Good-night, Jane.’ … She kissed me, and I her, and we both soon slumbered.”

findings.claim: “Jane stays for six more years and rises to become a teacher.”
findings.truth: Jane is at Lowood eight years in all — six as a pupil, two as a teacher — and Helen dies in her first year.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 10: “I remained an inmate of its walls … for eight years: six as pupil, and two as teacher.”

findings.claim: “Jane’s reply is the novel’s most famous assertion of female equality: ‘I am no bird…’”, placed after Rochester's proposal.
findings.truth: Plot order is reversed. The speech comes before the proposal and ends “which I now exert to leave you”; Rochester proposes ten lines later.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 23: “I am no bird…” at line 11691, “I ask you to pass through life at my side” at line 11701.

findings.claim: “Bertha sets three fires in the novel.”
findings.truth: Two: the hangings of Rochester's bed, and Thornfield on the final night.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 15 and ch. 36 (“she set fire first to the hangings of the room next her own…”).

findings.claim: “Jane responds sharply when he calls her ‘plain’: ‘I don’t think, sir, you have a right to command me.’”
findings.truth: Wrong trigger. Rochester has just claimed a right to be masterful because he is “old enough to be your father” and better travelled.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 14, lines 6102-6117.

findings.claim: Key fact: “Blanche is Rochester’s test of his own feelings… he proves to himself that Jane’s intelligence and integrity matter more” (also flashcard 11).
findings.truth: Rochester's own stated reason is to make Jane jealous. He separately spread a rumour that his fortune was small, which exposed Blanche.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 23: “I feigned courtship of Miss Ingram, because I wished to render you as madly in love with me as I was with you”; “I caused a rumour to reach her that my fortune was not a third of what was supposed”.

findings.claim: “Jane’s refusal to be his mistress later in Volume II”.
findings.truth: The refusal is chapter 27, the first chapter of Volume III.
findings.evidence: Three-volume scheme: Vol. II runs ch. 16-26, Vol. III begins at ch. 27.

findings.claim: “Jane dresses in plain white and writes of ‘a sense of something different’.”
findings.truth: Fabricated quotation — the phrase is nowhere in the novel. The real ch. 26 detail is the mirror: “a robed and veiled figure, so unlike my usual self that it seemed almost the image of a stranger”.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 26, lines 13275-13278.

findings.claim: “Rochester hurries her to the church ‘without pausing’.”
findings.truth: Fabricated quotation, and he does pause at the churchyard wicket. The real phrase is “hurried along by a stride I could hardly follow”.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 26, lines 13322-13326 and 13339.

findings.claim: “Her prose breaks into exclamations and second-person address — ‘Reader, it was irksome’.”
findings.truth: Fabricated quotation. There are seven “Reader,” addresses in the novel and this is not one of them. The ch. 27 address is “Reader, I forgave him at the moment and on the spot.”
findings.evidence: Gutenberg line 13815; “irksome” appears three times, never with “Reader”.

findings.claim: Flashcard 5: “What three-word exclamation does Rochester use to half-admit the charge?”
findings.truth: “Bigamy is an ugly word” is five words.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 26, line 13516.

findings.claim: “both were fair complexioned and slender…”
findings.truth: The text reads “slenderly made”.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 29, line 15400.

findings.claim: “his sermons are ‘stern, almost condemning.’”
findings.truth: Fabricated quotation. The sermon passage gives “stern allusions to Calvinistic doctrines”.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 30, lines 16279-16282.

findings.claim: Flashcard 3: “Which simile does Brontë use to describe St John Rivers?”
findings.truth: “a cold cumbrous column” is a metaphor, as lesson 7 of this same unit correctly says.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 34, line 18180: “but, at the fireside, too often a cold cumbrous column, gloomy and out of place.”

findings.claim: Rochester: “I have known you, Jane, only a few minutes, and already I feel my old hope of life is returning.” In five places: lesson 6 content, lesson 6 practice question 3, lesson 6 flashcard 6, and twice in lesson 7 (quotation banks).
findings.truth: Fabricated quotation — “hope of life” returns no match in the novel. Replaced with the real ch. 37 line: “Jane, I ever like your tone of voice: it still renews hope, it sounds so truthful.”
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 37, line 20597.

findings.claim: “at Moor House she is the independent heiress (‘I care for myself’)”, repeated in lesson 7 flashcard 4 and lesson 8 (“she resists … St John (‘I care for myself’)”).
findings.truth: “I care for myself” is chapter 27, spoken at Thornfield while refusing Rochester. Jane's refusal of St John is “I scorn your idea of love”.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 27, line 14634; ch. 34, line 18882.

findings.claim: Flashcard 11: “Which postcolonial critic and book reframe Bertha’s silencing?” answered “Jean Rhys, Wide Sargasso Sea (1966).”
findings.truth: Jean Rhys is a novelist. The lesson's own critic is Spivak.
findings.evidence: Lesson 7 content_html names “Jean Rhys and Gayatri Spivak” separately.

findings.claim: “OCR’s 40-mark question gives you an extract plus a prompt to start with it and then explore the whole novel.”
findings.truth: The paper sets one extended response from a choice of two: an extract-based question making links to the whole text, or a discursive question with no extract. The lesson taught the extract question as the only option.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/english-literature-J352.md section 3a.

findings.claim: Four practice extracts carry the wrong volume: lesson 4 questions 3 and 6 label chapter 27 “Volume II”; lessons 7 and 8 both label the chapter 23 “poor, obscure, plain, and little” speech “Volume I”.
findings.truth: Vol. I is ch. 1-15, Vol. II ch. 16-26, Vol. III ch. 27-38. Ch. 23 is Volume II and ch. 27 is Volume III. The unit uses this scheme consistently elsewhere.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg chapter line map; every other volume label in the unit checks out.

findings.claim: Practice question 6 extract: “Diana and Mary, to whom I dilated on my hopes and feelings, warmly caressed me. I could now be — what to them I had been — a real sister.”
findings.truth: Fabricated passage — “dilated on my” and “caressed me” return no match. Replaced with the real ch. 33 line on finding her cousins: “Glorious discovery to a lonely wretch! This was wealth indeed! — wealth to the heart! — a mine of pure, genial affections.”
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 33, line 17825.

findings.claim: Flashcard 12: “What disease sweeps Lowood and kills Helen Burns?” answered “Typhus.”
findings.truth: Typhus sweeps the school; Helen dies of consumption. The lesson body says so, so the card contradicts its own lesson.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 9: “her complaint was consumption, not typhus.”

findings.claim: “only Helen and St John survive into the closing pages”.
findings.truth: Helen dies at Lowood in chapter 9. The sentence means the two models remain in play, but a student could read it as Helen still being alive. Left alone — the next sentence says all three figures are memorialised.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 9.

findings.claim: The extract in practice question 1 quotes John Reed as saying “you are a dependant”.
findings.truth: The Gutenberg text prints “dependent”. This is an edition spelling variance, not an error; British print editions use “dependant”. Not corrected.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 1, line 355.

findings.claim: The unit punctuates “no net ensnares me:” with a colon in every one of its five appearances.
findings.truth: The Gutenberg text has a semicolon. Edition punctuation varies and the unit is internally consistent, so it was left alone rather than changed in five places.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 23, line 11691.

summary: Eight lessons checked against the Gutenberg text and the OCR J352 spec. Two unit-wide labelling faults: all 48 practice questions were typed a Shakespeare essay, and all 48 mark ladders were malformed. A third unit-wide fault: the author's name is misspelt Brönte 211 times in lessons 2-8. The marks (40), the closed-text 2-hour paper and the timing were already right, no per-AO mark split appears anywhere, and no lesson claims 30 marks, 45 minutes, a two-part question or a compulsory extract — but lesson 8 taught the extract question as the only option when the paper offers a choice of two. The real content faults are eight fabricated quotations (the worst repeated five times across two lessons), Helen Burns's last words wrong in a knowledge check and a flashcard, a flashcard teaching that typhus killed Helen when the lesson body says consumption, and four practice extracts filed under the wrong volume. 289 edits written; three LOW items left as notes.
